summary: This document requires that TLS clients and servers never negotiate the use of RC4 cipher suites, for all TLS versions. It updates RFC 5246, RFC 4346, and RFC 2246.

plainLanguage.summary: A secret code called RC4 turned out to be too weak. This says computers must never use it to protect connections.

questions: why was rc4 banned in tls
what happens if a client only offers rc4
which tls versions does rfc 7465 update
subtitle: TLS clients and servers must never negotiate the RC4 stream cipher, in any TLS version.

tldr.problem: RC4 is a stream cipher that was widely supported and often preferred by TLS servers, but it has long-known weaknesses and recent attacks use biases in its keystream to recover repeatedly encrypted plaintexts.
tldr.mechanism: Clients must not offer RC4 cipher suites in the ClientHello, servers must not select one, and a server must end the handshake if a client offers only RC4 suites.
tldr.outcome: RC4 can no longer be used with TLS 1.0, 1.1 or 1.2. The RFC updates RFC 5246, RFC 4346 and RFC 2246, and is itself updated by RFC 8996.

today: RFC 7465 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2015. It has not been obsoleted, but it is updated by RFC 8996. It updates RFC 5246, RFC 4346 and RFC 2246.

sections.title: Why RC4 Had to Go
sections.content:
RC4 is a stream cipher. The RFC notes that it is widely supported and often preferred by TLS servers, yet it has long been known to have a variety of cryptographic weaknesses.

Recent cryptanalysis exploits biases in the RC4 keystream to recover plaintexts that are encrypted repeatedly. The RFC says these results are on the verge of becoming practically exploitable: they currently require 2^26 sessions or 13x2^30 encryptions. Its conclusion is that RC4 can no longer be seen as providing a sufficient level of security for TLS sessions.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a lock that lets a patient burglar learn a bit more each time you use it. After enough tries the burglar can read your secrets, so you should stop using that lock.

sections.title: The Three Rules
sections.content:
The RFC uses RFC 2119 requirement words and makes three changes to TLS, which apply to all TLS versions it covers (RFC 5246, RFC 4346 and RFC 2246).

  • TLS clients MUST NOT include RC4 cipher suites in the ClientHello message.
  • TLS servers MUST NOT select an RC4 cipher suite when a client sends such a suite in the ClientHello.
  • If a client offers only RC4 cipher suites, the server MUST terminate the handshake. It MAY send the insufficient_security fatal alert.
sections.plainLanguage: Clients must not ask for the weak lock, servers must not pick it even if asked, and if the only thing offered is the weak lock, the server ends the conversation.

sections.title: How This Changes the Handshake
sections.content:
In TLS, the client lists the cipher suites it supports in its ClientHello and the server picks one. This RFC removes RC4 from both sides of that choice: the client must not list RC4 suites, and a server that sees one anyway must not choose it.

If that leaves nothing acceptable, the server does not fall back to RC4. It ends the handshake, optionally with an insufficient_security alert, so the connection fails instead of running with a weak cipher.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like ordering from a menu. The weak dish is taken off the menu, and if it is the only thing you ask for, the waiter says sorry and nobody eats.

sections.title: The Prohibited Cipher Suites
sections.content:
Appendix A lists the 18 RC4 cipher suites defined for TLS. They cover several key exchange families, including RSA, anonymous Diffie-Hellman, Kerberos, pre-shared key, and elliptic-curve variants (ECDH, ECDHE).

Examples are TLS_RSA_WITH_RC4_128_SHA, TLS_RSA_WITH_RC4_128_MD5 and TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_RC4_128_SHA. Suites with a 40-bit key, such as TLS_RSA_EXPORT_WITH_RC4_40_MD5, are on the list too.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC includes a full list of every menu item that uses the weak lock, so nobody has to guess which ones are banned.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The security section is a single statement: the document helps maintain the security guarantees of TLS by prohibiting RC4-based cipher suites, which do not provide a sufficiently high level of security.
sections.plainLanguage: Taking away the weak lock keeps the whole door as safe as people expect it to be.
